All means calculated to advance the sanitary condition of the people have lately received much consideration. A new registered brick, denominated " the universal ventilating brick," would appear to lie deserving of the attention of architects and others employed in the erection of buildings. The objects sought to be attained by the use of the brick are þÿ lirst, a of years' imprisonment in irons, and in one the building, so as to ensure perfect dryness of the walls, and complete security against the dry rot. Secondly, the easy and economical diffusion of artificial heat in hot-houses and other buildings of that description ; and, thirdly, a saving in the cost of the brickwork" itself to the extent of upwards of thirty per rent. The brick is also stated to he particularly well adapted for paving kitchens, lobbies, Are. A c., as it admits of a free current of air under the flooring, and ensures perfect freedom from damp; and in the case of new buildings, by the application of artificial heat, the walls may he dried and the building rendered habitable within an exceedingly short space of time,

Gone to Earth. þÿ The If amriigh Borsenhaele states the cold to be so severe at Kamitchatka, that the governor had been compelled to quit his usual residence at St. Peter and St. Paul, to bury himself under the earth þÿ that is to say, he has retired to his subterranean palace, which is 20 metres below ground, and is capable of accommodating 200 persons. This palace is perpetually lighted by lamps. Most wealthy private persons have dwellings of this kind, but it is rarely cold enough to induce them to lice thither for refuge.

A Lea rnt.d ami Scientific Joker. þÿ The Leeds Intelligencer relates an anecdote of Professor Sedgwick. He was engaged to dine at Scarborough. þÿ A little outside the town he took out his geological hammer, and began to break up some of a heap of stones in order to observe their construction. The professor, who was not very well dressed, was exceedingly busy when a lady drove up in a carriage, and. after asking lum several questions as to w hether he could earn a living by his occupation, how many children he had, Ac., to all of a\ liich Sedgwick replied with great gravity, gave him a shilling, w hich he pocketed with great apparent thankfulness and humility. On his arrival at Scarborough, whom should he meet at the table of his friend but the lady in question ? The lady did not recognise him in his more civilised attire, but expressed her conviction that she had seen his face before "O! yes, ma'am," replied Professor Sedgwick, "don't you remember speaking to a man on the road, asking how many children he had, and giving him a shilling? Here it is," continued he, pulling the coin out of his pocket, "and I'll keep it for your sake." So saying, the lively professor whipped the shilling into his pocket again, and very soon charmed the lady and the company with his extraordinary conversational powers.

TMieam i i. Event it N xri.r.s.þÿ A dreadful explosion and tire occurred at Naples, on the 6th Fobr'y., w liich threatened extensive destruction. The cellars of the Darsens, or closed port, extend from the water's edge to a considerable distance under the principal buildings of

the city, including the magnificent palaces of the Princes of Salerno and Capua, and the King's palace. In these cellars were warehoused 277,000 cantara of coal, and on the morning of the 2nd an explosion of fire-damp took place underneath the palaces of the Princes of Salerno and Capua, which threw down large portions of the walls, and it was with great difficulty that the inhabitants escaped. Miraculous Escape. þÿ It has been said that reality frequently exceeds romance, and nothing can better exemplify the axiom than a notice of the providential and almost miraculous oseaoe i which Captain C. \\ . Andrew s, of the Caroline, whaler, which ship touched here on Saturday, lias lately experienced. Captain Andrews, in this instance, whilst in pursuit of a w hale, a few days since, look the place of the harpooner at the bows of the boat. On closing with the whale he struck home, and the monster flew immediately downwardlike lightning, but by some means the bight of the rope caught the ancle of Captain Andrews, and whirled him overboard. His sensations at Ibis moment may be imagined, but cannot be described. Descending rapidly into the depths below, be bad yet sufficient presence of mind to retain his hold of the knife; but the pressure of the water was so great that both bis arms were drawn over bis bead, and lit found it impossible to get them down to release himself, llappily the w halt , from some cause or other, ceased to run, and Captain Andrews was enabled to sever the rope below bis ancle, and ascended to the surface totally exhausted. The depth to which he descended must have been from fifteen to twenty fathoms, from the time he took to bring himself to the surface again. He found his ancle cut to the bone and otherwise severely injured. Probably an accident like the one here noticed lias never one," remarks the New Emu \nd\V \sii- occurred before in which the sufferer
has ever escaped with life, and, bad not Captain Andrews happily retained bis bold of the knife, be most certainly would have perished. þÿ Ceylon Times.

The British Government and the Kepi uliu or Costa Rica. þÿ \ copy of the treaty of friendship, commerce, and navigation between her Majesty and the Republic of Costa Bica (presented to Parliament,) was printed on Monday. The treaty w as signed at San Jose on the 27 tli November last, and the ratifications were exchanged in London on the 20th ult. " There shall be perpetual amity between her Majesty, her heirs, and their subjects, and tile Government of the Republic of Costa Rica and its citizens." There is to be a reciprocal freedom of commerce between the two countries ; vessels are to enter into the harbours, but not to carry on the coasting trade, in which trade national vessels only are permitted to engage. Any favour, privilege, or immunity in matters of commerce and navigation granted by

one state to the other sliall be gratuitously, or on the same footing, as agreed upon between the two countries. Mutual forbearance is to be exercised in matters of religion, Ac. Among the sixteen articles contained in tiie treaty is one to the effect that the Government of the Republic of Costa Rica in order to co-operate with her Majesty for the abolition of the slave trade, engages to execute perfectly the laws of the Republic, which prohibit in the most effectual manner all persons inhabiting within the territories of the Republic from taking any share in such trade.

The Etymology of Blankets. þÿ AN bile Edward III., in 1337, repeated bis invasion of Scotland, and " ravaged 'lie country with great fury, burning Aberdeen and many similar towns," as the historians tell us ; and while he was engaged in raising an army to invade France in 1338, exacting from the impoverished English people all their wealth to waste it in war, borrowing money from all foreign princes who would lend him, pawning the English crown w hich made him a king, that lie might still further extend destruction over fertile France; when, in the bat ties which our historians and poets have so minutely recorded and loi'tilv sung of, swords, clashed with swords, and battleaxes rung upon coats of mail, the warrior-heroes of England mingling their blood and backed heads w ith the blood and backed beads of the warriorheroes of France, there was a servant of mankind making a noise in Bristol, which was ol infinitely greater service to England than the entire conquest of Europe would have been. This was Thomas Blanket. The noise he mathwas not that of the clashing sword, but that of the dashing shuttle. His pur pose was not to destroy what bis country already possessed, but to give his country what it did not \rt possess þÿ id AiNkets, a covering of comfort to go to bed with, to sleep under, that it might, be refreshed in sound sleep, and rise in health and strength to its daily work, ol making mankind happier by being hap pier itsclt. Thomas Blanket was soon imitated by bis neighbours, who, like

him, set up looms in their own houses, and made woollen cloth like that which he made. The cloth was named by bis name ; and to this day, through all time ia this country, will the name be know n, though nothing cise is known of this weaver than that he was the first to introduce the blanket manufacture in England.

sets sons inclined to an ambitious turn of Handwriting. þÿ Some time ago, perrniml thought it indicative of an intellectual or literary disposition to write an unreadable hand ; and we have heard men boast that they wrote so as not to be understood. This is an odd kind ot success, and a very vulgar one to boot. A rapid hand may indicate a habit of writing, and therefore a familiarity with pursuits more or less intellectual ; hut not to be able to write both well and fast is a defect of skill, and can in no way he twisted into an ornamental trait. To write so that your correspondent cannot decipher you, is silly as regards your own object in writing, disrespectful as regards him. Not to perceive that certain words which do not derive elucidation from the contest, such as technical terms and proper names, need peculiar distinctness, is a mistake of dulness. We do not mean to say that all men who write badly are dullards, or we might he confuted by a storm of illustrious autographs; hut we do mean, that when a man intends to make you understand an idea, has a pen in li is hand for the purpose, and fails for want of capacity to make the letters of the alphabet, that þÿman s intellect is asleep. þÿ Spectator.

A few years ago all the sentences were summary, and the punishmentsdrcadful. Capital punishments were astonishingly frequent, and seemed to he regarded with the utmost indifference by all classes of Mussulmans. It was not often that you could go by tbe gate of the Seraglio without seeing a ghastly exhibition of bleeding heads : somewhere or otherþÿ in the capital or in the provinces þÿ the yataghan or the bowstring were constantly at work. If low continued to he designated as a a Turk made any observation about these sanguinary proceedings, it was

a very powerful King; and then he would slightly shrug lib shoulders and talk about kismet (destiny.) They were all familiarised with t lie sight of blood, and this no doubt tended to increase the popular ferocity. On the accession of the present Sultan, a milder spirit on the part of Government began to manifest itself. As executions became rare þÿ and they became rarer every yearþÿ the Turks began to consider them with emotion, and even with horror ; the old indifference to the sight of blood departed from them : they spoke with astonishment of th<' frequent executions they had been in the habit of witnessing a few years ago. The ease of the unhappy Armenian renegade will he still ftct.li in the recollection of Christendom. þÿ This man had renounced his religion uid embraced Islam, and after living fi r s lim' vears as a Mussulman lie had renounced the Prophet and sought a re-

Great efforts were made to save this þÿman life: s the young Sultan was known to he averse to his execution, hut the Sheik ul Islam, and all the fanatics of Constantinople, insisted that, in so solemn a case as this, the law must take its course ; and in the end the poor Armenian was led out to be executed. The Terrs as they were and as they are. þÿ The Turks over in Constantinople certainly looked much less like Turks, and were far more civil than in 18-8. They were incomparably less picturesque and imposing in their outward appearance. The forced change of costume has transformed them into a rather mean, shabhy-looking people. But for t lie glaring red fez z (a mean, ungraceful head covering in itself), they might pass for Franks who employed had tailors and seldom got their clothes finished, A blue frock-coat, buttoned up to the chin, and dirty duck pantaloons, not wider than we wear them, were the prevailing fashion. In my time Sultan Mahmoud had made war on flowing, bright-coloured robes, and a fierce attack on the loose, baggy nether garments of the Mussulmans: hut still the prejudice was strong in favor of an amplitude of trousers, and a shabby fel-

It has even been asserted with more than common audacity or ignorance that the objections to the renewal of the armistice of the 10th of .Julv had been raised by Denmark. But the facts of the case are so important that we shall produce them with greater minuteness and accuracv.

Yet that is the condition to by force of arms. That Denmark which Lord Palmerston apprehends, and with reason, that the objections of the Frankfort Commission will be addressed; for although Prussia lias not the impudence openly to disavow her own signature to the articles and arrangements of the 10th ol July, she has hitherto successfully employed her intlucncc at Frankfort to prevent the Federal Commission from acknowledging

ATI 8 the armistice and the preliminaries þÿ nay, she has even prevented the Commission from receiving the credentials of M. de Below, Danish Commissioner to the Confederation on behalf of ins Sovereign as Duke of Holstein, and member of that body, although the appointment of such a Commissioner was expressly provided for on the part of all those States which accepted the Federal Convention of the 30th of September in last year. By the most captious pretences such as an affected irritation at an expression in the King of þÿDenmark speech s from the throne, and by the lowest subterfuges, the Prussian Ministers are seeking to evade the peremptory obligations of their signature. But since they are so afraid of the conditions to which they themselves were happy to accede under the pressure of the blockade of last summer, we shall proceed to show more fully than has yet been done what those conditions are, and we shall leave the w orld to whether they are of a be evaded with impunity. þÿ The public terms of the convention are already well known. They consist in ihc occupation of a portion of .Schleswig, south of a particular line, by a corps of (3000 Prussians, whilst t lie north is garrisoned by a smaller detachment of Swedes. The administration of' the country is in the hands of a mixed commission, of which Col. Hodges is a member, and the respective military forces are bound by Art. 11 to support that commission þÿ a stipulation which has constantly been evaded with the

greatest insolence bv the Prussian commandant, General II ahn. In addition to these terms, the preliminaries of peace, signed at the same time, expressly provided that þÿ the Duchy of Schleswig þÿ shouldhave a separate Constitution þÿ lor its Legislature and its internal adþÿ ministration, but w ithout being united þÿ to the Duehv of Holstein, and leaving þÿ untouchedthe political union which þÿ attaches the Duchy of Schleswig to þÿ the Grow n of þÿDenmark. That is the fundamental condition, accepted by Prussia on behalf of Germany, w hich stands above all further dispute. But in addition to this language of the protocol, secret articles w ere agreed 1o by Prussia. By these it was provided Mat in the event of a refusal on the part of the Duchies and of the Schleswig-Holstein army to accept the armistice, and of resistance on their part to its execution, with or without the assistance of any of the German contingents the King of Denmark should be at liberty to use all the means in his pow er to conquer them should not invoke the assistance of any foreign Power, but that Prussia in order to contribute as far as in her lay to the strict execution of the armistice, would not only withdraw from the Duchies all the Prussian troops, and especially these stationed in the South of Schleswig by the terms of the armistice, but would also recall without delay on the first demand of the Danish Court, all Prussian

officers, including General Bonin, now serving in the Schleswig-Holstein armv. The King of Prussia further engaged to employ all his influence in the Germanic Confederation to induce that body to perform all the duties resulting from the Federal acts of 1815 and 1820 for the restoration of peace and of the lawful authority of tlie Sovereign in the Duchy of Holstein in consideration of which promise Denmark engaged not to extend her military operations beyond the frontier of Schleswig. The 'other secret articles, being of less general interest, we shall not at present produce. But, in our judgement there is a moment at .which articles of this nature, cease to he secret and that is when they are violated : for otherw ise the breach of faith which is their sanction would remain unknown. We assert, then lhat the Prussian Government has materially deviated from the terms, both patent' and secret, to which it acceded on the 10tii of July, by interposing frivolous and unnecessary delays in (lie negotiation lor the definitive pence þÿ b\ w ithholding that support which il bad engaged give to the administrative Cum to mission þÿ hy thwarting instead of aiding Denmark in (lie suppression of the insurrection by her influence at Frankfort and elsewhere þÿ and by keeping alive the hopes of a party she professed to have renounced, in one word, the object of Denmark has obviously been t lie termination of hostilities on the terms recommended by the mediator ; the object of Prussia lias been to play

the game best suited to the supposed temper of the Erfurt Parliament, and to humour t lie culpable designs of a party which is to contribute to her own supremacy over the rest of the Confederation. . . vip. A very erroneous impression lias been adopted by some of the German organs in this country, that England lias bet u employed in some intrigue, more or less successful, to defeat the ini cut ions of Russia on this question. We believe that statement to be wholly unfounded and that Lord Palmerston and the Russian Government have been pursuing the same object by nearly the same means þÿ both of them have recommended the Danes to submit to terms, and both of them have sought to make the Germans concede and observe reasonable conditions. In 1 lie former of these objects they have succeeded ; and w e trust that all the Powers interested in this dispute will take effectual measures to bold the Prussian Government to llu conditions it subscribed on the 101 i i of July. That armistice was concluded in order to obtain by persuasion or by force the submission of the Stadtholderate ; it has served only to enable that insurrectionary body to recognize its forces and bold a more imperious language to its Sovereign rejecting the very conditions which England herself lias laboured to obtain for them. Whether this armistice between Denmark and Germany be renewed or not there is therefore great reason to fear that

hostilities will recommence between Rcniimrk ami the Duchies not without the connivance of some parties in Germany. Our own duty and our own interest hi this question are more than ever dear; and we are satisfied that if the þÿ1 russian Government had been made to feel that the settlement of this dispute on the principles to which it lias formally agreed is peremptorily required of it by England, Russia, and France, all obstacles must have disappeared. þÿ slot og AYhcn we consider the effects of another blockade on our vast commerce with the north of Europe, amounting to ten millions a year, and the inconvenience to which the mere apprehension of such a danger exposes the mercantile interests of England, we have a right to use all the powers which former treaties and recent mediation have conferred upon the Qt f.i:n of this country for the purpose of terminating a contest which has arisen from the intrigues of a foreign fiction in the Danish dominions, abetted by neighbouring a state for its own sinister objects. Since Lord P u.mi:k>to.\ is so sensitive to the rights and interests of British subjects, lie will find in the Gallic a proper field for his most energetic remonstrances, and even perhaps for the display of his naval activity. It js now established by the admissions of the Government in the House of Com 1110ns that the delay in the negotiation and the peace has arisen on the side of Prussia not of Denmark, and we therefore hold the Government bound, in conjunction with the other allies ol Den-
mark, to see that justice is promptly done by the execution of all the articles of the convention of July, which were Mailed under our mediation, and must be fulfilled on our demand.

Floor lire West Indian, Burbadoes Feb. 11. On Friday we had tiro satisfaction to receive the first and second January mails. The first, were brought hy the Steamer E vut.E, front St. Thomas, and the second from Southampton, hy the 'I'M. \\ c find hy the Tim us of the 11th, 1 hut the Avon arrived on the lOtli Jiinunrv, after a rough passage across the \lluntic. It will he remembered that .Iritis Inniss, l'.sqr., Sonus, Esqr., and M ss Yi;\, were passengers in the \ v on, audit will he gratifying to Mr. t n n ts'.s many friends to learn that he had reached England safely. On the s ilrject of the Royal Mail Steam Racket Company the Times remarks: þÿ "The present arrival furnishes a fresh instance of the satire and complete inu leqitacy of the system of Steam communication now maintained with the I'.n ilic and West Indies, hy means of the Steamers of fhe Royal Mail Steampack I Company. The Avon left (.'Ita-

<n & $ a AT 1 « grcs for Southampton about the same time as the American steamer Crescent City for New York; and whereas the former vessel litis only readied her destination on the ICtli of January, the advices hy the Crescent Cilv were received tit Liverpool on the 24th of December, thus exhibiting a difference in time of at least 1(5 days. It therefore follow s, that if the $1,250,000 brought by the Avon had been shipped hy the Crescent City for New York, and there transferred to the Liverpool steamer, an equal saving in the time occupied by the transit of these remittances would have been effected, and a vast deal of anxiety avoided hy both merchants and underwriters interested in the arrival of this valuable freight. The cause of such inconvenient results lias been frequently alluded to and explained in this journal, and it has been clearly shown to he produced solely by the extraordinary route adopted from the Isthmus of Panama to England, as well as hy the repeated and vexatious stoppings of the steamers to take up intermediate mails. On the present occasion we lintl that the Avon, after leaving Chagres, called, as usual, at Carthagena, Jamaica (where site remained four days with the Pacific mails and freight on hoard), JaenicI (llayti), 1'orto Rico, and SR. Thomas. No wonder, therefore, at the fact of the Avon's advices from the American continent having been forestalled by a lew merchants possessing the foresight to direct their correspondence by way of New York, or at the significant passenger-list of this

steamer showing about 25 cabin-passengers from 41 ports of call. It is clear that, so far as the Pacific purls, Jamaica and the llavannah, tire concerned, the vv hide of the passengers and specie traffic must speedily leave this line for the more expeditious one from Chagrcs and Jamaica to New York. We trust, however, that some steps will he speedily taken to stay the evil before it shall have become impossible and irreparable, and that the Government will cede to overtures which have been made for a change of route of the steamers. < >n the other hand, the success, nay, the very existence of the Royal Mail Company, depends upon the speedy preparation of steamers of much greater speed with which to perform the Ytlantic voyages with increased regularity and rapidity. The present position of this company in regard to t tic energetic and powerful competition which litis recently sprung up on the part of the Americans, is far from creditable to the enterprise of a great British commercial association, or favourable to that development of British commerce w hich ought at till events to keep pace with the events of the times, he they ever so rapid or unexpected. The company once possessed 14 steam-ships of 1,81)0 tons burden, but now, front repeated losses, there are hut ten, and although the hitter number is the number prescribed by the terms of the contract with the Government, yet if another ship were to be wrecked the company would not have sufficient ves-

sels to work the contract for w hich so large a subsidy is annually devoted hy the public Exchequer. It' the company had regularly replaced its lost ships by others, those vessels would now have been available to meet the opposition of the American steamers, hut, its it is, the interests of the British merchants must continue to suffer till ships of greater speed have been built, and more than a year w ill necessarily elapse ere suitable steamers can lie got ready for the sern ice. YVe make these remarks because w e understand that the new steamers, ot 2,500 tons and 800 horse-power, intended to he constructed for the Royal Mail Company, have been held in abeyance from some cause or other connected with an indisposition of Ihe Government to promise a renewal of the contract which expires in 1852. Should the company vv ait till 1852 ere deciding upon the necessary steps to place tinnew arrangements in operation, it may he safely predicted that by that time the necessity for any British line of steamers at till the YY est Indies and South America w ill have entirely ceased, for the w hole of the traffic will have been diverted into Ymcrica channels. Two years more of steam navigation on its present footing will effectually give the Americans such a preponderance and advantage its will effectually negative any subsequent effort of the West India Mail Company to recover their lost position. \\ ith a judicious change of route, and a more rapid communication, quickly decided upon and carried into

effect, the traffic front the whole of Spanish Ymcrica, the Pacific, and the W est Indies to Europe, will he retained in its legitimate channel ; and prosperity and success can only be anticipated for this company, if a line of policy be adopted equaling in energy and enterprise that displayed by our American rivals iu the important and vastly increasing commerce of the west."

From the New Y'uik Herald, Feb. 10, 1850. Tim vi. Tit tp or 'nit. Nrw Wori.d on the Ot i. v\ þÿ R \< i. with in it Northerner. On Saturday, the new steamboat Now YVorld made her trial trip on the ocean, starting with the Northerner, at 3 o'clock in the afternoon and only returning yesterday morning, at I o'clock. Her trial trip in company w ith the Georgia, on the 2Mb of January, was considered satisfactory, as far as rapid sailing in smooth water was concerned: though even in that respect she had hardly fair play, starting immediately upon being launched, and before her engines and boilers were improved hy a little use. But it was not ascertained by that trip what her ocean qualities were, and her builder and principal owner, YY If. Browne, re- . solved to trv her on " deep, deep sea." Accordingly he appointed Saturday for the purpose, and invited a select party of friends to accompany him on an excursion with fhe Northerner, advertised to sail for Charleston on Saturday. Even this trip, however was not a de-

cisive test of her rapacity to buffet tlie billows, and ride triumphantly over them in rough weather, for the water was almost as smooth as glass outside, barring that natural glorious swell of the ocean, which is the most beautiful thing in nature, and always to lie found even in the calmest weather, when there is " not a breath the blue waves to curl." At half past 2 o'clock the New World, after taking on board the excursion party at the foot of Twelfth street, steamed up the East River for some distance, and then turning, proceeded to the Battery, where she rounded and headed up the North River, intending to return in time to start with the Northerner from the foot of Courtland street. The Northerner, however, went sooner than was anticipated, sailing sharp at 3 o'clock. The New World, on perceiving this, immediately put about and gave her chase. She was then about a mile and a quarter ahead. At 4 minutes past 3, the New World passed the dock of the Northerner, and in 2J minutes more she passed the Northerner herself when abreast of Robin's Reef, at the near extremity of Ktatcn Island, thus heating the Northerner four miles an hour. At 34 minutes past 3 o'clock or just half an hour from the time Ihc New World passed Courtla... d street she cleared the telegraph at the further extremity of Staten Island, being at the rate of upwards of 23 miles ar. hour. She was performing 20 revolutions to the minute when she was in chase of the Northerner; afterwards she performed 21 revolutions, which was

the utmost speed she attained, with 34 inches of steam on. At 5 minutes past 1 o'clock she passed the Sandy Hook Eight, just an hour and one minute Irom .he time she left the foot of Courtland street. She was then stopped, and the company were entertained to a magnificent dinner by .Mr. Browne. After waiting 20 minutes, the Northerner being Mtill behind, it w as proposed to go to sea 70 or SO miles more, so as to make a trip ot 100 miles out ami I'M! in. i acre being plenty of fuel and provisions on board, the proposition was agreed to and song, and mirth, and wine, and speeches were the order of the night. She kept steady a coarse south by west (steering by the compass) till SI o'clock, v, hen her engineer and ow ncr calculated we were fully l'»0 miles to sea, and put hack, reaching the Battery at hall past 3 o'clock, and landing at Twelfth street at I o'clock, making an average speed out and in, (allowing for stoppages) of 17 miles per hour, ller owner was anxious for rough water; hut it was only when she reached her dock that it began to blow fresh." The night, up " to that time, was very hazy and thic k, so that it was not safe, meeting so many vessels as she did, to put her to her full speed coining hack. She burned about 1 1 tons of coal from the time she left the foot of Twelfth street till she rct irticd, a period of I I hours. She is an exceedingly beautiful model, and the moment the spectator sees her, he is impressed with a feeling of her speed,

> j » 71 a (0 li 02 ATI 5-. just as when looking at the proportions of a thoroughbred racer. She is sharp fore and aft, and has her buoyancy chiefly in the centre, ller sides are rather flat, or what may he termed well-sided. But her lines are beautiful, and where she enters the water, and where she leaves it, there is as little foam as we ever saw at the stem and stern of a boat going with her speed. Her engine worked as sweetly as we ever saw any engine work, 'and adds another laurel to the Archimedes Works of Dunham Co. lis operation j was superintended by Mr. Joseph Belknap, li "aftsman of the firm. The engine is on deck. The wheels are considerable behind the centre. A promenade deck runs fore and aft, as in the Georgia and Ohio. Her exterior and saloon are very neatly painted, and the iatur is titled lip very handsomely. .She proceeds to San Francisco in a few days, and her owner is confident she will perform the distance in a time far shorter than it was ever yet accomplished þÿ in fact in a time that will astonish the community. Among those who took part in this trip were Captain Floyd, of the Washington, and Captain Sherman, the oldest of our captains, who owned and commanded the first steamer on Lake Erie. In order not to interrupt the narrative of the sailing, we did not insert the toasts and other proceedings at the dinner, in their proper place, in order of time, but shall subjoin such a sketch here as our space will permit.

ENGLAND. The House of Commons having resolved itself into a committee on the Australian colonies, Lord J. Russell said he felt it would be very convenient if he took that opportunity of making a statement to the house of the colonial policy of the Government. Having stated the history of the acquisition of colonies to this country, he said it had been the policy of the Government from an early period to make a monopoly of the trade between this country and its colonies, though of late years that policy had undergone considerable alteration. Great changes had been at various periods introduced into the government as well into the commercial policy of the colonies down to last year, when the repeal of the navigation laws put an end to that monopoly which had been first encroached upon by the liberal and comprehensive measures of Mr. lluskisson. Some of those colonies had rapidly grown into wealth and population, and even the W est Indies had gone through the change from slavery to freedom much better than might be anticipated, if they were to judge by the amount of produce which they had shipped to this country. To those who alleged that we should abandon our colonies he would reply that they w ere a portion of the strength of the empire, and independent of the moral obligation which rested upon us to promote the happiness and civilisation of communities with which we had so long been connected, it was to be remembered that they afforded to our commercial marine harbours in all ports

ot the world, very beneficial in time of peace, but absolutely indispensable in time of war. Many of them were so situated, surrounded by hostile tribes of natives, that, if we were to withdraw our protection, they must inevitably look for protection from other powers. The noble lord having gone at considerable length into the historv of some of the colonies, proceeded to describe what was intended to be done with the Cape of Good Hope and other colonies. With respect to the Cape of Good Hope he proposed to give to it n representative government, to consist of an Elective Council and a Legislative Assembly, the constituency to consist of persons possessed of a certain amount of property. The Legislative Assembly should be reelected every five years, and the Council every ten years, but one-half to be re-elected every five years. Sir W. Molesworth said that in most of the observations which fell from the noble lord in the introductions of Ins speech with respect to the past history ot our colonics and the policy under which they had been governed, lie entirely agreed ; but he regretted to learn from the other parts of the noble lord's speech, that it was the intention of the Government to adhere to their present objectionable policy for the government ot our vast colonial empire. Since the present Colonial Secretary came into office, not only had the colonics been

1 misgoverned, but for the last four years the house and the public had been kept in ignorance of the proceedings, and no satisiaetory account could be obtained of the conduct of the Government. In the Cape ot Good Hope, in Van Diemen's Land, and other colonies, there was a general feeling of dissatisfaction with our colonial policy, and in many of them the people accused the Government of breach of faith. A complete reform in their colonial policy was imperiously demanded; and no hope of such a reform had been held out in the speech of the noble lord that evening. The honorable baronet, after reviewing at considerable length the condition of most of the Britisli colonies, concluded by expressing his disappointment at the speech of the noble lord, and his dissatisfaction with the present colonial policy of the Government. Mr. Hi me said that he believed it would not be possible at the present moment to point out a single one of our colonies w hich was not in a state of discontent, and a premium would be given to that discontent when it should be discovered that the colony which had successfully resisted the British Government was the very one which had obtained from that Government the most liberal constitution. Mr. Adderley said there was one redeeming clause in the constitution for Australia þÿ the one which gave to the council the power of altering that constitution, though even that was verv nun h qualified by a subsequent clause, which said that all such alterations must

From the liiustrated London News, Feb. 16 Important Discovery. þÿ Mr. Smith, of Dcanston, in Gloucestershire, has made an important discovery in the treatment of the fleeces of sheep, whereby the fleece of the living animal is rendered repellant of water by a simple and clean process ; so that the sheep are defended from the pernicious effect of wet, whilst the natural emanations from the body remain unchecked, and the growth and quality of the wool are improved. The effect of this waterproofing lias been practically tested on some of the most exposed sheep-walus m Scotland, and with singular success. This process, it is expected, will effectually supersede the laying with tar, and butter, and other salves, at one-third of the cost, whilst the wool will be preserved white and pure. Though the laving or salving of sheep hitherto has been applied chiefly to flocks on mountainous and exposed situations only, it is believed that the new mode of treatment w ill he found beneficial to flocks fin the most sheltered and southern paslures, and that it will go far to prevent or mitigate that destructive disease þÿ the rot, which is neither more nor less than dysentery, caused by the continuance of wet weather, w hereby the fleeces of the sheep become soaked with rain, and produce the same effect as is produced on man by wet clothing. It is also presumed that this mode of treatment traordinary commissioners to different will lead to the successful introduction of the Spanish sheep and the Alpaca, which are known to have suffered from

The riotous display in Paris last week has been followed by a corresponding lull, and all is as tranquil, dull, and uninterestiiig as in any peace-loving cummou-sciisc city in existence. For lack of unpleasant tacts, however, the Parisians have taken to vexatious forebodings, grounded on alleged intention on the part of the Government to make an important modification of the military commands into which France is divided. Vt present France consists ot seventeen mand of a general officer, military divisions, each under who the com- makes ins reports to the Al inister of \\ ar direct. It is now proposed that these seventeen divisions shall be abolished, and that France shall he formed into either four or live divisions, each ot which is to he placed Under th eon mand of a Lieuten-

3 © US & a X ATI3« ant-General, who is to have an almost unlimited command, and who can, whenever he sees occasion, place the whole of his division under martial law. The divisions are to be called according to their positions þÿ north, south, east, west, and centre. These great divisions are to be sub-divided, and placed under the command of Major-Generals, who will make their reports to the Lieutenant- Generals in command. On the slightest appearance of disorder, or even the " slightest o indication of agitation," in vanv one of these five divisions, the Lieutenant-General in command can immediately declare it in a state of siege. Some appointments have been made which are stated to he in accordance with this plan; viz: General dc Castellane lias been appointed Commander-in- Chief of the 12th military division (Bordeaux), and the 14th and 15th divisions (Nantes and Henries) are also placed under his command. General Kostolan is appointed to the command of the 8th, !)th, and I Ot ii, military divisions (Toulouse, Perpignau, and Montpclier ; and the Oth military division (Besan<;on) is added to the 5th military division (Lyons), and left under the command of General Geneau. In other respects the journals arc occupied w ith the approaching elections. The clubs meet daily to talk over the candidates they shall propose, but nothing definitive as to the persons selected has yet been determined upon. The advices from the provinces are somewhat more favourable. The agitation has in a degree subsided, and it is

Dr. Cantwell, Roman Catholic Bishop of Meath, in a letter to the Tablet, states that lie has over a thousand pounds a year at his disposal, for the use of a Catholic University, should one be established in Ireland. þÿ Ibid. þÿ OOO Attempting too Much. þÿ There is such a thing in this world as attempting too much. With all the haste to get rich, there is still more haste to " show off" what one is really not worth. It people could conceive the ridiculous altitude which they place themselves in by attempting an appearance which nothing short of the most exorbitant hopes could justify, they would be prone to draw their horns in a bit, and to practise a little more contentment and a little more honesty. They remind us of the villa of a gentleman, which, though its rooms were but closets, presented such a gallant outside, that we will hastily describe it. It had turrets two foot in breadth, with battlements like the side crust of a Christmas goose-pie. To complete the appearance of a castle, you enter by a drawbridge, which exactly resembles the lid of a travelling trunk. To the right of the house is a puddle, dignified with the name of a harbour, and defended by two redoubts, under cover of which lies a vessel of the size of an ordinary bathing tub. We might put more in the picture, but we think we have said enough to show that the gentleman of t lie villa, like a great many others, made too much outside show. Oi course no one can licip smiling at this weak a.ssumption of importance. Cut your coat ad-
cording to your cloth, is a homely hut Common-sense adage. The man who is honest with himself, who assumes nothing but what is just, will not be apt to attempt too much.

Water Drinking. þÿ Dr. II. Johnson, in his recent work on Domestic ILiiko- I'ATiiv, makes the following remarks : þÿ I am decidedly opposed to the indiscriminate drinking of large quantities of cold water. One cannot understand in what manner these large imbibitions are to operate so as to lie useful to the animal economy. W e know precisely what becomes of the water soon after entering the system: we can trace exactly what course all this water must take what channels it must traverse þÿ between its entrance and its exit. We are perfectly well acquainted with certain physiological effects produced by it after it lias been received into the system. It dilutes the blood, it lowers the temperature, and therefore diminishes the vital power of the stomach ; it puts certain sv stems ot capillary blood-vcsseis on the stretch, to the great danger of bursting, and it overtaxes the kidneys. I have si en two very had cases, which were fairlv attributable to the excessive drinking of water. Thus, llicii, it seems there are certain wellunderstood and very obvious injuries

a UL <0 It >0 3 2: AT32 which the large imbibiiton of water cannot fail to iniliet, while the supposed benefits to accrue from it are altogether mystical, problematical, unintelligible. þÿ The quantity of water which each person should drink during the day must always depend ob his own feeling, lie may always drink when the doing so is agreeable to his sensations ; when it is repulsive, never."

How to Feed Horses. þÿ An intelligent farmer in the neighbourhood informs us that he effects an immense saving by having bis oats crushed before giving them to bis horses. The expense of the operation is not more than 1«. per sack, while the difference of cost in the keep of the animals is fully þÿone-half. Formerly each horse would eat a sack of oats in a week ; now, the same quantity suffices for a fortnight, with considerably less hay than before, while, at the same time, the animals both go through their work better and have a finer appearance. Tiie reason is obvij ous ; the food is better digested ; and thereby a further evil is prevented, namely, the scattering over the soil, in the shape of manure, of a quantity of partially decomposed grain, which becomes a prolific source of weeds. The subject is well worthy of the attention of all practical agriculturists. The plan is no new one ; and there fore we must conclude that it is not ignorance, but indolence or prejudice, that stands in the way of its general adoption.

From the first of his reaching the town, he paid attention to several females, and made offers which were declined. At length a young girl, who
obtained her livelihood by delivering milk for sale, listened to bis overtures ; but as her mental qualifications were scarcely deemed high enough for the þÿ can in S.-ce;. ' betook the precaution

to send her to a boarding school and other places of instruction, to qualify her to be a help- mate for him. In due time she was married in the nantc of Itlack. Fortune seemed to smile upon the Scotchman, for his business visibly increased, and also his means of enjoyment þÿ a dwelling of a higher class being occupied by the couple. At length there seemed to be a turn to this good fortune, and most people were surprised to hear that a fiat in bankruptcy bad issued against Alexander Black. The fiat was prosecuted ; it was under the old bankrupt law, when the examination of the bankrupt was taken in presence of the creditors generally in the town where the bankrupt resided. While A. þÿBlack examination s was proceeding the sheriff's officer in attendance, having reason to believe that ali the property that Black possessed had not been given up, left the room, and went in search of the þÿ Huddersfield- wife, to whom he represented that he had been sent by her husband þÿ for that þÿmoney, and that unless it was sent, he (the husband) would have to be committed to York Castle. This representation operating on the fears of the poor distracted wife, she went to the hiding place, and produced £1100 in gold, which she delivered to the sheriff's officer, and which was by him speedily laid before the assembled creditors, to their great astonishment and delight. This bankruptcy being worked to the end, and a ccrificatc obtained, our Scotchman commenced the world again in the same line of

business þÿ borrowing £200 to enable him to do so from the very sheriff's officer w ho had so cunningly stript him of the secretted £1100; and whose faith in þÿBlack integrity s seems to have been of an extraordinary kind. It should here be mentioned that the affair of the £1100 so preyed upon the mind of the Huddersfield wife, that she was for a considerable period an inmate of a lunatic asylum; and a lew years after her release she died, leaving our Scotch townsman apparently a widower. A few weeks ago he also died þÿ and then came the revelations we have now' to detail. Fortune had again smiled upon him, and having some £l.»00 to dispose of he willed small portions amongst some members of the family he had married into in þÿHuddersfield some other portions to his housekeeper, and the rest to parties whom he named, resident in Scotland, and whom he described as his nieces and nephews. To this will, his old friend, the þÿsheriff s officer, was made one of the executors. There is at present living at Elton, near Stockton, a woman called Mary Benton, who is now in her 120th year. She was born at Cockfield, where the registry of her baptism maybe seen in the books of the parish church, bearing date February 12, 1731. lier faculties are good, and she is able to perform most of her household duties without assistance.

A young man, near Wakefield, playing with a young girl, she hid his spade. He took rip a loaded gun and shot her. It was at first supposed that he had done it maliciously, but it now appears that the misfortune was the result of a foolish and dangerous frolic. The girl is recovering, and the man lias made his peace with her by promising to marry her as soon as she is well enough. The face of the poor girl is much disfigured.

nn?#- Tlie soil of Ireland belongs in fee to fewer owners than any equal area in Western Europe, except Spain. It has been demised in many eases to tenants for life, who share the property with the owners in fee ; and neither class can do with it what they like. The whole land has long been hound in legal fetters and complicated interests. Besides this, inos' of the proprietors have long been peculiarly embarrassed ; their estates were mortgaged, and, according to their rank and condition, they required all the rent they could possibly exact. To this end they had not prevented, if they had not encouraged, the division of their properties into a great number of small holdings. Almost destitute of manufactures and commerce, the hulk of the Irish relied exclusively on the land for their subsistence : they competed tor it in the fiercest manner: and, in order to obtain it, promised and paid the most exorbiant rent, being contented to live on the smallest possible quantity of the coarsest food. In 1847, the number of holdings, according to Captain Lareom's report, after many thousands had been merged in others or left altogether waste, was 729,971. I am not acquainted with the exact number when the law was enacted'; but, in 1841, the holdings of more than one acre and less than five acres exceeded those of 1847 by 184,510. From that fact, 1 infer that the total number of holdings in 1838 could not have been much less Mian 1,000,00(1. At the period, then, of nacting the Poor-Law, the land was

owned by a few embarrassed proprietors ; and it was divided into an immense number of small holdings, the great majority of which were tilled by men in the very lowest condition of civilisation. Of a population of 8, (MI0, 000, it was estimated that 2,000,000 were in such a state of destitution as partly to subsist by mendicancy and to require relief. The applicability of the Poor- Law to that condition of society is the point to be considered. At that time ail opinion prevailed that small holdings were inconsistent with good agriculture, and that a greater net produce and higher rents would lie obtained Irom large than from small farms. From di persons possessing authority, the landlords had continually been advised to diminish the number and enlarge the size of the holdings, to treat the land on the commercial principle, and the process of eviction and agglomeration had in many cases commenced. The number of vagrants was before fearful : to prevent vagrancy and guard against its increase by evictions, the law was partly justified ; by taking away the pretext for vagrancy, eviction was encouraged. . I have already shown you, by the immense number of evictions in the last few years, that the law in fact gave a terrific impulse to flic process. Clearing estates of the people has latterly been the great object of the landowners, and the chief recommendation of statesmen and public writers of authority. þÿ The landlords may have been misled ; thev may, in this ease, as in many others,

havo'inisunderslood their own interests ; hut there. cannot be a doubt that, since the Poor-Law was passed, the condition both of Ihc mass of the people and of the landowners lias been much deteriorated. The latter have been impoverished the former, when spared, have been famished down to hopeless degradation, and, in. many cases, actually

3 tr. y starved to death. It is my business specially to show how the law contributed to this disastrous result. It is usually described as a law to make property, and particularly the property of the landlords, support poverty. But. the heart of man þÿ particularly the heart of a legislator, who can by no means divest himself of our natural selfishness þÿ is wonderfully deceitful ; and the law, which is nominally said to lie for the support of the poor, at the expense of property, is found, when examined, to be really for their extirpation, at the expense of industry, its principle is to make those who have anything share it with those who have nothing. It is avowedly intended to make property support poverty. Following the law of Elizabeth, or rather the amended Poor-Law of 1834 þÿ which in 1838 had not developed ail its sinister effects, and was supposed, at least by its authors, to be an admirable law þÿ the Legislature adopted a workhouse test, and levied rates on the occupiers as w ell as on the landowners ; it taxed industry as well as land ; it levied rates on profit as well as rent, for the support ot the destitution that already existed, and that might be created by the clearing process ; it enacted that" half of the rate should be paid by the tenant. By nominally providing an asylum for the evicted þÿ which was wholly inadequate, and which the poor wretches, from custom and feeling, were slow to enterþÿ it satisfied the consciences of the evicting landlords; and, by throwing half the

burden on the occupiers, it really made the unevicted, industrious tenantry pay a large part of the expense of clearing the landlords' estates. That arrested the progress of industry in Ireland. þÿ The law fell cruelly on the class of occupiers, particularly on the small occupiers struggling out of the mire of general poverty, and thrust them back to be smothered.

It is perfectly clear that the very smallest occupiers could pay no rates, and the landowners having been made responsible for their rates, eviction was further encouraged by a desire to get rid of none rate-paying tenants, and to acquire tenants w ho, occupying larger holdings, would pay rates." The law, therefore, said be for the protection to ot the people, was really a scourge to them. With accelerated activity eviction went on before the famine, and as it went on the hardens on the industrious occupiers increased. Every increased rate occasioned by an increase of jumpers diminished their means; till many of those who jiaid rates lost the ability to pay, and added to the burdens of those who continued to pay. Thus the law ensured a continual increase of pauperism, and lessened the means of supporting it. Complaints of that were rife long before the famine of 184(1. All the numerous occupiers of small holdholdings who found it difficult to live before they were subjected to a jioorrate, then found it impossible. In many cases their jirojierty w as sold off for the rates, and a serious blow given to the national industry. The dearth of 184(1, jnirtly the consequence of that, found all energy paralyzed ; and when the hand of the .State, full of wealth, was held out to relieve tlieni, dispirited by the gradual increase of the terrible demands of t lie collectors, they one and all nearly gave up the unprofitable pursuit of farming, and threw themselves on the State

for help. We hear in our time a great deal of judgments ; but if ever there were a judgment, the utter jirostration ot the Irish, consequent on the failure ot a harvest greater than usual, was a judgment for the law which deprived
the industrious occupiers of their jiroperty, stojmed their exertions, and almost rooted hope out of their hearts.
